case: Bloom names Zadig. The shelved Voltaire romances (PG 35595, PG 18972) carry no translator's name, and the St. Hubert Guild set is a revised Smollett. This is a fresh, credited translation by the man who did Racine for Bohn, and the title page says so: 'A new translation by Robert Bruce Boswell'. One volume, the tales Bloom means. UPDATE 2026-11-03: Lane B also found PG 18972 (1749) and PG 35595 (1889), both with anonymous translators; Boswell stays the pick because he is named.

work: Voltaire, Letters concerning the English Nation (2nd edition, with large additions)
translator: not named on the title page (attributed to John Lockman)
printing: C. Davis and A. Lyon, London, 1741
case: The English version came out in 1733, before the French one, so this is close to the book's first form, not a late translation of it. But the title page names no translator, and the lane rule excludes unnamed translators. Shelve with the credit 'translator unnamed; attributed to John Lockman' only if you waive the rule for this book. An earlier 1733 copy (nby_758806) has no text layer.

Bloom's 'The Mandrake'. Copyright 1927, so US public domain since 2023, and the scan is the 1927 printing. A clean, credited translation by a known critic and translator. Only the play; Clizia and Belfagor are not in it.

work: Bruno, Spaccio della bestia trionfante, or the Expulsion of the Triumphant Beast
translator: not named (traditionally attributed to William Morehead)
case: The only pre-1931 English Spaccio. Two problems: no translator is named, and the OCR of the opening leaves is noise, so the title page could not be read from the text layer. Needs the scan image read before it can even be put to you properly. Hold.

work: Tirso de Molina, The Love-Rogue (El burlador de Sevilla)
case: The only pre-1931 English Trickster found. But Kemp calls it 'a poetic drama transmuted from the Spanish', which reads as a free verse adaptation, and the lane rule excludes retellings. Cut unless you want a stand-in for Bloom's title.

printing: Thomas B. Mosher, Portland, Maine; copyright 1896, this scan a 1904 printing
case: Bloom names Sylvie. Title page: 'Translated from Gerard de Nerval by Lucie Page'. Andrew Lang's sonnet and a few of his Nerval versions are prefixed. The same translation is PG 40492, which could be the source instead of the scan. The contents also list Aurélie material; check whether that is Aurélia (Bloom 368) before claiming it.

Bloom's Laforgue is 'Selected Writings'; the Moralités are his prose masterpiece and this is their first English book. 'Edited & translated by Frances Newman', copyright 1928, so US public domain since 2024. The archive.org server returned an error once and then served the text.

work: Novalis, Hymns and Thoughts on Religion
case: Covers Bloom's Novalis half way: the spiritual songs and the religious fragments (the 'Aphorisms' side), with a biographical sketch. It is NOT the Hymns to the Night; no pre-1931 English Hymns to the Night was found yet. Hastie was a Scottish divinity professor, so this sits well beside lane A's shelves.

work: Boileau, Le Lutrin: a Mock-Heroic Poem in Six Cantos
translator: John Ozell (with an account of Boileau by Nicholas Rowe); credit to be confirmed on the scan
printing: R. Burrough, J. Baker, E. Sanger and E. Curll, London, 1708
case: The Lutrin is the model Pope's Rape of the Lock answers, and this is the English version Pope's circle read. The title page puts Rowe's name under the prefixed account; library cataloguing gives the verse to Ozell. The credit needs a look at the scan before shelving.

work: Boileau, The Art of Poetry (in The Art of Poetry: the Poetical Treatises of Horace, Vida and Boileau)
translator: Sir William Soame, revised by John Dryden (Horace tr. Francis Howes, Vida tr. Christopher Pitt); edited by Albert S. Cook
case: The Soame-Dryden Boileau is the classic English version, and Cook prints it beside Horace and Vida with notes, three neoclassical poetics in one volume. Better than the bare 1683, 1710, 1715 and 1755 printings, which are also on archive.org.

First English Salammbô, credited and dedicated by the translator. The Chartres Everyman found on archive.org is a 1956 reprint and fails the pre-1931 printing rule. UPDATE 2026-11-03: Lane B's PG 1290 names no translator; Sheldon stays the pick.

translator: John Stirling (pen name used by T. B. Peterson's translator)
case: Credited on the title page, 'complete and unabridged'. But Peterson's Zola translations have a reputation for softening, and 'John Stirling' is a house pen name, not a person you could look up. The 1922 Knopf Nana says only 'Translated from the French', so it fails the named-translator rule. Keep this one if you want Nana at all.

work: Zola, The Assommoir (the prelude to Nana)
case: The famous Vizetelly edition, the one that got Henry Vizetelly prosecuted. No translator is named, so it fails the lane rule as written. Its 'unabridged' claim is also doubtful. UPDATE 2026-11-03: Lane B also found PG 8558 and 8600, which name no translator, and a second Vizetelly scan, assommoirprelud00zolagoog.

translator: Henry G. Alsberg and Winifred Katzin
printing: Liveright, New York; copyright 1926, but this scan is the eighth printing, July 1937
case: Text is US public domain (published 1926). But the only scan found is a 1937 printing, and the lane only shelves pre-1931 printings. Hold until a 1926 to 1929 printing turns up, or rule that a later printing of a PD text is fine. UPDATE 2026-11-03: Lane B is adding The Dybbuk on its own branch, judging the 1937 printing a straight reprint of the 1926 Alsberg-Katzin text. Lane C's hold is dropped and Lane C will not shelve it. Whether later printings of pre-1931 texts are acceptable is still Adam's call (DIGEST-C).
Right book, right date, but the scan has only 3 page texts and no full text or PDF, so it cannot be fetched. Recheck later.

work: Flaubert, Three Tales (incl. A Simple Soul)
printing: copyright 1924 (Knopf), but this scan is a New Directions printing from after 1936
case: The text is US public domain, but the scan is a post-1930 printing, so it fails the lane's printing rule. Hold for a 1924 Knopf scan. UPDATE 2026-11-03: Lane B's PG 1253 and 10458 name no translator.

work: Calderón, Dramas: Tragic, Comic and Legendary, vol. I (The Constant Prince; The Secret in Words; The Physician of His Own Honour)
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. Bloom's 'The Doctor of His Own Honor' is the Physician of His Own Honour, which the contents list at p. 281. MacCarthy is already the house Calderón (denis-maccarthy shelf), but this 1853 volume is not on it. It brings The Constant Prince with it, which is a Calderón Bloom does not name but which is famous in its own right.

work: Ronsard, Songs and Sonnets of Pierre de Ronsard
printing: Houghton Mifflin, Boston and New York, 1903
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. Title page: 'Selected & translated into English verse by Curtis Hidden Page'. A selection, but the only all-Ronsard English book found. Payne's Flowers of France (held) has some Ronsard among many poets.

From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. The only English Nicomède found. It is a Restoration EEBO scan with a long-s, poor OCR, so it reads badly until cleaned. Keep it only if you want Bloom's lesser Corneilles at all. The Cid (PG 14954, Mongan) is already held on singles-fiction-4.

work: Voltaire, Toleration and Other Essays (incl. the Poem on the Lisbon Disaster)
printing: G. P. Putnam's Sons (Knickerbocker Press), New York and London, 1912
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. PG names McCabe as translator, and the contents include the 'Poem on the Lisbon Disaster' at p. 255. It covers Bloom's title and adds the Treatise on Toleration. McCabe has a shelf already (mccabe), but it holds his own books, not this.

work: Goethe, West-Eastern Divan in Twelve Books
printing: J. M. Dent, London and Toronto, 1914
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. The only complete English Divan before 1931. Title page read: 'Translated by Edward Dowden', 1914, published posthumously. The scan is from microfilm and the OCR is noisy at the start, so expect cleanup.

translator: not named in the PG file (thought to be the Bohn translation; its note says 'Now first translated into English')
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. The PG file names neither a translator nor a printing, so it fails the named-translator rule. Better to find a credited pre-1931 printing, such as Bohn's Dramatic Works, on archive.org.

printing: not stated in the PG header
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. Coleridge's Piccolomini and Death of Wallenstein are already held (coleridge shelf). This is the missing first part, so it completes the trilogy, and PG credits 'Translated by James Churchill'.

From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. Title page read: 'Translated by D. H. Lawrence', Blackwell 1929. A pre-1931 printing, and US public domain (first published 1925). A Bloom title translated by a Bloom author.

printing: Jonathan Cape, London: first published 1925, this scan the Travellers' Library reissue of 1928
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. Title page read: 'Translated by D. H. Lawrence', with the printing line 'First published 1925, re-issued in the Travellers' Library 1928'. Pre-1931 printing. Lawrence's own introduction is included.

From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. The only English Bécquer poems before 1931 found. The held 'Romantic Legends of Spain' is his prose, not the Rimas.

translator: not named in the PG file (the Doré-illustrated edition)
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. No translator is named, so it fails the lane rule. The Commelin 'Atala' is a poetic dramatization, already rejected. Look for a credited scan of the Doré edition, which was Cassell's, translated by James Spence Harry.

translator: various, each poem credited to its translator
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. A many-hands anthology. Every poem carries its translator's name, which is how the house already treats Bohn collections. No Hugo poetry is held.

printing: Estes and Lauriat, Boston (1864 on the title page; probably a later issue of the 1864 translation)
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. PG header and title page both credit A. Baillot. Hugo on Shakespeare is a natural fit for the shelves.

work: Alfred de Musset, The Complete Writings (10 vols)
translator: various per volume: vol. 4 'done into English by Dr. Edmund Burke Thompson'; vols. 1-2 poems by Andrew Lang, Marie Agathe Clarke and others (IA catalogue; not read on the page)
printing: Edwin C. Hill, New York, 1905 (subscription edition)
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. One set covers two Bloom entries: the Poems (vols. 1-2, with the Nights) and Lorenzaccio (vol. 4, title page read). The held 'Confession of a Child of the Century' is probably vol. 8 of the same family. Shelve the Bloom volumes only, not all ten, under the no-bloat rule.

printing: M. Walter Dunne, New York and London, copyright 1904
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. This is the same Dunne text Lane C found on archive.org. It names no translator, so it fails the lane rule; the only credited alternative found (Brentano's 1922) names Ranous as editor only. Waive the rule or go without.

work: Pushkin, The Bakchesarian Fountain and Other Poems by Various Authors
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. Only one Pushkin narrative poem, padded out with Derzhavin and others. Thin cover for Bloom's 'Narrative Poems'. Panin's Poems (1888, PG 54991) is already held on singles-plays-poetry-2 for entry 573.

printing: text copyright 1930 (Boni); this scan is a Grove Press printing with a 1956 introduction
case: From Lane B's handoff (docs/review/bloom/lane-c-handoff.md, branch claude/project-thread-yu0x73, commit e4a93ce9); access and credit rechecked by Lane C. It fails two lane rules: 1930 printings are held, and the scan is a 1950s Grove printing whose del Río introduction is still in copyright. Hold for a 1930 Boni scan and a ruling on 1930.
